On the well posedness and large-time behavior of higher order Boussinesq system

Roberto A. Capistrano–Filho Address: Departamento de Matemática, Universidade Federal de Pernambuco (UFPE), 50740-545, Recife (PE), Brazil. Email address: capistranofilho@dmat.ufpe.br, roberto.capistranofilho@ufpe.br , Fernando A. Gallego Address: Departamento de Matemáticas, Universidad Nacional de Colombia, UNAL, Cra 27 No. 64-60, 170003, Manizales, Colombia Email address: fagallegor@unal.edu.co, ferangares@gmail.com and Ademir F. Pazoto Address: Institute of Mathematics, Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (UFRJ) P.O. Box 68530, CEP 21945-970, Rio de Janeiro (RJ) Brazil. Email address: ademir@im.ufrj.br
Date: 2018-08-27-a
Abstract.

A family of Boussinesq systems has been proposed to describe the bi-directional propagation of small amplitude long waves on the surface of shallow water. In this paper, we investigate the well-posedness and boundary stabilization of the generalized higher order Boussinesq systems of Korteweg-de Vries–type posed on a interval. We design a two-parameter family of feedback laws for which the system is locally well-posed and the solutions of the linearized system are exponentially decreasing in time.

Key words and phrases: 
Boussinesq system of higher order, Stabilization, Möbius transform, Critical length, Fifth order KdV–type system
2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary: 93B05, 93D15, 35Q53

1. Introduction

1.1. Presentation of the problem

J. L. Boussinesq introduced in [8] several simple nonlinear systems of PDEs, including the Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) equation, to explain certain physical observations concerning the water waves, e.g. the emergence and stability of solitons. Unfortunately, several systems derived by Boussinesq proved to be ill-posed, so that there was a need to propose other systems similar to Boussinesq’s ones but with better mathematical properties. In this spirit, an evolutionary version of the Boussinesq systems was proposed in [14, Eqs. (4.7)-(4.8), page 283]:

(1.1) {ηt+ux+16​β​(3​θ2−1)​ux​x​x+1120​β2​(25​θ4−10​θ2+1)​ux​x​x​x​x+α​(η​u)x+12​α​β​(θ2−1)​(η​ux​x)x=0ut+ηx+β⁡[12​(1−θ2)−τ]​ηx​x​x+β2​[124​(θ4−6​θ2+5)+τ2​(θ2−1)]​ηx​x​x​x​xα​u​ux+α​β​[(η​ηx​x)x+(2−θ2)​ux​ux​x]=0,\begin{cases}\eta_{t}+u_{x}+\frac{1}{6}\beta(3\theta^{2}-1)u_{xxx}+\frac{1}{120}\beta^{2}(25\theta^{4}-10\theta^{2}+1)u_{xxxxx}\vskip 2.84544pt\\ \hskip 170.71652pt+\alpha(\eta u)_{x}+\frac{1}{2}\alpha\beta(\theta^{2}-1)(\eta u_{xx})_{x}=0\vskip 5.69046pt\\ u_{t}+\eta_{x}+\beta\left[\frac{1}{2}(1-\theta^{2})-\tau\right]\eta_{xxx}+\beta^{2}\left[\frac{1}{24}(\theta^{4}-6\theta^{2}+5)+\frac{\tau}{2}(\theta^{2}-1)\right]\eta_{xxxxx}\vskip 2.84544pt\\ \hskip 142.26378pt\alpha uu_{x}+\alpha\beta\left[(\eta\eta_{xx})_{x}+(2-\theta^{2})u_{x}u_{xx}\right]=0,\end{cases}

where η\eta and uu are real function of the real variables xx, tt. The small parameters α>0\alpha>0 and β>0\beta>0 represent, respectively, the ratio of wave amplitude to undisturbed fluid depth, and the square of the ratio of fluid depth to wave length, both are assumed to be of the same order of smallness. Finally, τ\tau represents a dimensionless surface tension coefficient, with τ=0\tau=0 corresponding to the case of no surface tension and the velocity potential at height 0≤θ≤10\leq\theta\leq 1. For further discussions on the model and different modelling possibilities, see, e.g. [4, 5, 7, 12, 14, 23].

The goal of this paper is to investigate two problems that appear on the mathematical theory when we consider the study of PDEs. The first one is the global well-posedness, in time, of system (1.1), which is so-called fifth order KdV–type system. Another problem is concerned with boundary stabilization of the linearized system associated to (1.1).

First, we consider the following system, carefully derived by (1.1) in a short Appendix at the end of this paper,

where a>0a>0, b>0b>0, a≠ba\neq b, a1>0a_{1}>0, a2<0a_{2}<0, a3>0a_{3}>0 and a4>0a_{4}>0, with the following boundary conditions

(1.6) {ηt+ux−a​ux​x​x+b​ux​x​x​x​x=0,in ​(0,L)×(0,∞),ut+ηx−a​ηx​x​x+b​ηx​x​x​x​x=0,in ​(0,L)×(0,∞),η(x,0)=η0(x),u(x,0)=u0(x),in ​(0,L),\begin{cases}\eta_{t}+u_{x}-au_{xxx}+bu_{xxxxx}=0,&\text{in }(0,L)\times(0,\infty),\\ u_{t}+\eta_{x}-a\eta_{xxx}+b\eta_{xxxxx}=0,&\text{in }(0,L)\times(0,\infty),\\ \eta(x,0)=\eta_{0}(x),\quad u(x,0)=u_{0}(x),&\text{in }(0,L),\end{cases}

with the boundary conditions given by (1.3).

Then, the following questions arise:

Problem 𝒜\mathcal{A}.

Does E⁡(t)→0E(t)\to 0 as t→∞t\to\infty? If it is the case, can we find a decay rate of E⁡(t)E(t)?

The problem might be easy to solve when the underlying model has a intrinsic dissipative nature. Moreover, in the context of coupled systems, in order to achieve the desired decay property, the damping mechanism has to be designed in an appropriate way to capture all the components of the system.

Before presenting an answer for Problem 𝒜\mathcal{A}, it is necessary to investigate the global well-posedeness of the full system (1.2)-(1.3). Thus, the following issue appears naturally:

Problem ℬ\mathcal{B}.

Is the fifth order KdV–type system globally well-posed in time, with initial data in Hs​(0,L)H^{s}(0,L), for some s∈ℝ+s\in\mathbb{R}^{+}?

1.2. Some previous results

It is by now well know that mathematicians are interested in the well-posedness of dispersive equation which depends on smoothing effects associated to datum (initial value or boundary value). The well-posedness of the initial value problem for single KdV equation and single fifth order KdV equation was deeply investigated. For an extensive reading on the subject see, for instance, [6, 11, 13, 15, 24] and the reference therein. In contrast, the well-posedness theory for the coupled system of KdV–type is considerably less advanced than the theory for single KdV–type equations [4, 5, 21, 22, 23]. The same is true for the stabilization properties.

In additional, other interesting problem, as mentioned previously, in the stabilization problem. Problem 𝒜\mathcal{A} was first addressed in [18] for a Boussinesq system of KdV-KdV type

(1.7) {ηt+ux+(η​u)x+ux​x​x=0in ​(0,L)×(0,T)​,ut+ηx+u​ux+ηx​x​x=0in ​(0,L)×(0,T)​,η⁡(x,0)=η0​(x)​, ​u​(x,0)=u0​(x)in ​(0,L),\left\{\begin{array}[c]{lll}\eta_{t}+u_{x}+(\eta u)_{x}+u_{xxx}=0&&\text{in }(0,L)\times(0,T)\text{,}\\ u_{t}+\eta_{x}+uu_{x}+\eta_{xxx}=0&&\text{in }(0,L)\times(0,T)\text{,}\\ \eta(x,0)=\eta_{0}(x)\text{, \ }u(x,0)=u_{0}(x)&&\text{in }(0,L),\end{array}\right.

with the boundary conditions

(1.8) {u⁡(0,t)=ux​x​(0,t)=0,in (0,T),ux​(0,t)=α0​ηx​(0,t),ux​(L,t)=−α1​ηx​(L,t)in ​(0,T)​,u⁡(L,t)=α2​η​(L,t),ux​x​(L,t)=−α2​ηx​x​(L,t)in ​(0,T),\left\{\begin{array}[c]{lll}u(0,t)=u_{xx}(0,t)=0,&&\text{in }(0,T)\text{,}\\ u_{x}(0,t)=\alpha_{0}\eta_{x}(0,t),\quad u_{x}(L,t)=-\alpha_{1}\eta_{x}(L,t)&&\text{in }(0,T)\text{,}\\ u(L,t)=\alpha_{2}\eta(L,t),\quad u_{xx}(L,t)=-\alpha_{2}\eta_{xx}(L,t)&&\text{in }(0,T),\end{array}\right.

where α0≥0\alpha_{0}\geq 0, α1>0\alpha_{1}>0 and α2>0\alpha_{2}>0. Note that, with boundary conditions (1.8), we have the following identity

dd​t​E​(t)=−α2​|η⁡(L,t)|2−α1​|ηx​(L,t)|2−α0​|ηx​(0,t)|2−13​u3​(L,t)−∫0L(η​u)x​η​𝑑x,\frac{d}{dt}E(t)=-\alpha_{2}|\eta(L,t)|^{2}-\alpha_{1}|\eta_{x}(L,t)|^{2}-\alpha_{0}|\eta_{x}(0,t)|^{2}-\frac{1}{3}u^{3}(L,t)-\int_{0}^{L}(\eta u)_{x}\eta dx,

which does not have a definite sign. In this case, first the authors studied the linearized system to derive some a priori estimates and the exponential decay in the L2L^{2}–norm. It is established the Kato smoothing effect by means of the multiplier method, while the exponential decay is obtained with the aid of some compactness arguments that reduce the issue to prove a unique continuation property for a spectral problem associated to the space operator (see, for instance, [2, 19]). The exponential decay estimate of the linear system is then combined with the contraction mapping theorem in a convenient weighted space to prove the global well-posedness together with the exponential stability property of the nonlinear system (1.7)-(1.8) with small data.

Recently, in [10], the authors studied a similar boundary stabilization problem for the system (1.7) with less amount of damping. More precisely, the following boundary conditions was considered

{η(0,t)=0,η(L,t)=0,ηx(0,t)=0,in ​(0,T)​,u⁡(0,t)=0,u⁡(L,t)=0,ux​(L,t)=−α​ηx​(L,t)in ​(0,T)​,\left\{\begin{array}[c]{lll}\eta(0,t)=0,\ \eta(L,t)=0,\ \eta_{x}(0,t)=0\ ,&&\text{in }(0,T)\text{,}\\ u(0,t)=0,\ u(L,t)=0,\ u_{x}(L,t)=-\alpha\eta_{x}(L,t)&&\text{in }(0,T)\text{,}\\ \end{array}\right.

with α>0\alpha>0. In this case, it follows that

dd​t​E​(t)=−α​|ηx​(L,t)|2−13​u3​(L,t)−∫0L(η​u)x​η​𝑑x.\frac{d}{dt}E(t)=-\alpha|\eta_{x}(L,t)|^{2}-\frac{1}{3}u^{3}(L,t)-\int_{0}^{L}(\eta u)_{x}\eta dx.

Proceeding as in [18] the local exponential decay is also obtained for solution issuing from small data. However, due to the lack of dissipation, the unique continuation issue for the linearized system can not be obtained by standard methods. In order to overcome this difficult, the spectral problem was then solved by extending the function (η,u)(\eta,u) by 0 outside (0,L)(0,L), by taking its Fourier transform and by using Paley-Wiener theorem. Finally, the problem was reduced to check for which values of L>0L>0 two functions are entire for a set of parameters. Then, the authors concluded that the stabilization properties holds if and only if the length LL does not belong to the following critical set

𝒩:={π​k2+k​l+l23;k,l∈ℕ∗}.\mathcal{N}:=\{\pi\sqrt{\frac{k^{2}+kl+l^{2}}{3}};\ k,l\in\mathbb{N}^{*}\}.

We point out that the same set was obtaned by Rosier, [19] while studying the boundary controllability of the KdV equation with a single control in L2​(0,T)L^{2}(0,T) acting on the Neumann boundary condition. This shows that the linearized Boussinesq system inherits some interesting properties initially observed for the KdV equation.

1.3. Main results and comments

In the present work, we address the problems described in the previous subsection and our main results provide a partial positive answer for the Problems 𝒜\mathcal{A} and ℬ\mathcal{B}. In order to give an answer for Problem ℬ\mathcal{B}, we apply the ideas suggested in [9, 10], therefore, let us consider

X¯3={(η,u)∈[H3(0,L)∩H02(0,L)]2;ηx​x(0)=vx​x(L)=0}.\overline{X}_{3}=\{(\eta,u)\in[H^{3}(0,L)\cap H^{2}_{0}(0,L)]^{2};\ \eta_{xx}(0)=v_{xx}(L)=0\}.

With this notation, one of the main result of this article can be read as follows:

Theorem 1.1.

Let T>0T>0. Then, there exists ρ=ρ⁡(T)>0\rho=\rho(T)>0 such that, for every (η0,u0)∈X¯3(\eta_{0},u_{0})\in\overline{X}_{3} satisfying

‖(η0,u0)‖X¯3<ρ,\|(\eta_{0},u_{0})\|_{\overline{X}_{3}}<\rho,

there exists a unique solution (η,u)∈C⁡([0,T],X¯3)(\eta,u)\in C([0,T];\overline{X}_{3}) of (1.2)-(1.3). Moreover

‖(η,u)‖C⁡([0,T],X¯3)≤C​‖(η0,u0)‖X¯3\displaystyle\|(\eta,u)\|_{C([0,T];\overline{X}_{3})}\leq C\|(\eta_{0},u_{0})\|_{\overline{X}_{3}}

for some positive constant C=C⁡(T)C=C(T).

In order to prove Theorem 1.1 we first analyze the linearized model by using a semigroup approach. Moreover, by using multiplier techniques, we also obtain the so-called Kato smoothing effect, which is crucial to study the stabilization problem. In what concerns the full system, the idea is to combine the linear theory and a fixed point argument. However, the linear theory described above seems to be unable to provide the a priori bounds needed to use a fixed point argument. To overcome this difficult, we consider solutions obtained via transposition method, which leads to consider a duality argument and the solutions of the corresponding adjoint system. Then, the existence and uniqueness can be proved by using the Riesz-representation theorem that gives, at first, a solution which is not continuous in time, only L∞L^{\infty}. The continuity is then obtained with the aid of what is known as hidden regularity of the boundary terms of the adjoint system. In fact, we prove that such system has a class of solutions which belong to appropriate spaces possessing boundary regularity. On the other hand, it is also important to note that identity (1.5) does not provide any global (in time) a priori bounds for the solutions. Consequently, it does not lead to the existence of a global (in time) solution in the energy space. The same lack of a priori bounds occurs when higher order Sobolev norms are considered (e.g. HsH^{s}-norm).

With the damping mechanism proposed in (1.3), the stabilization of the linearized higher order Boussinesq system (1.6) holds for any length of the domain. Thus, the second main result of this paper is the following:

Theorem 1.2.

Assume that α1>0\alpha_{1}>0, α2>0\alpha_{2}>0 and L>0L>0. Then, there exist some constants C0,μ0>0C_{0},\mu_{0}>0, such that, for any (η0,u0)∈X0:=[L2​(0,L)]2(\eta_{0},u_{0})\in X_{0}:=[L^{2}\left(0,L\right)]^{2}, system (1.6)-(1.3) admits a unique solution

(η,u)∈C0​([0,T],X0)∩L2​(0,T,[H2​(0,L)]2)(\eta,u)\in C^{0}\left(\left[0,T\right];X_{0}\right)\cap L^{2}\left(0,T;[H^{2}\left(0,L\right)]^{2}\right)

satisfying

‖(η⁡(t),u⁡(t))‖X0≤C0​e−μ0​t​‖(η0,u0)‖X0,∀t≥0.\|(\eta(t),u(t))\|_{X_{0}}\leq C_{0}e^{-\mu_{0}t}\|(\eta_{0},u_{0})\|_{X_{0}},\quad\forall t\geq 0.

In order to prove Theorem 1.2 we proceed as in [10, 18], i.e, combining multipliers and compactness arguments which reduces the problem to show a unique continuation result for the state operator. To prove this result, we extend the solution under consideration by zero in ℝ∖[0,L]\mathbb{R}\setminus[0,L] and take the Fourier transform. However, due to the complexity of the system, after taking the Fourier transform of the extended solution (η,u)(\eta,u) it is not possible to use the same techniques used in [10]. Thus, to prove our main result we proceed as Santos et al. [20].

For a better understanding we will introduce a general framework to explain the idea of the proof. After to take Fourier transform, the issue is to establish when a certain quotient of entire functions still turn out to be an entire function. We then pick a polynomial q:ℂ→ℂq:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C} and a family of functions

Nα:ℂ×(0,∞)→ℂ,N_{\alpha}:\mathbb{C}\times(0,\infty)\to\mathbb{C},

with α∈ℂ4∖{0}\alpha\in\mathbb{C}^{4}\setminus\{0\}, whose restriction Nα​(⋅,L)N_{\alpha}(\cdot,L) is entire for each L>0L>0. Next, we consider a family of functions fα​(⋅,L)f_{\alpha}(\cdot,L), defined by

fα​(μ,L)=Nα​(μ,L)q⁡(μ),f_{\alpha}(\mu,L)=\frac{N_{\alpha}(\mu,L)}{q(\mu)},

in its maximal domain. The problem is then reduced to determine L>0L>0 for which there exists α∈ℂ4∖{0}\alpha\in\mathbb{C}^{4}\setminus\{0\} such that fα​(⋅,L)f_{\alpha}(\cdot,L) is entire. In contrast with the analysis developed in [10], this approach does not provide us an explicit characterization of a critical set, if it exists, only ensure that the roots of ff have a relations with the Möbius transform (see the proof of Theorem 1.2 above).

The remaining part of this paper is organized as follows: In Section 2, we establish the well-posedness of the linearized system. We also derived a series of linear estimates for a conservative linear Boussinesq system which will we used to prove the well-posedness for the full system (1.2)-(1.3). Section 3, is then devoted to prove the well-posedness for the nonlinear system. In section 4, we prove an observability inequality associated to (1.6)-(1.3), which plays a crucial role to get second result of this paper, Theorem 1.2, proved in the same section. Finally, some additional comments and open problems are proposed in the Section 5. We also include an Appendix with a detailed derivation of the system (1.2).

2. Well-posedness: Linear system

The goal of the section is to prove the well-posedness of the linearized system. In order to do that, we use the semigroup theory and multiplier techniques, which allow us to derived so-called Kato smoothing effect. We also use the same approach to study a similar conservative linear Boussinesq system that will be used to study the full system (see, Definition 3.1).

2.1. Well-posedness: linear system

We will study the existence of solutions of the linear homogeneous system associated to (1.6), namely

(2.1) {ηt+ux−a​ux​x​x+b​ux​x​x​x​x=0,in​(0,L)×(0,T),ut+ηx−a​ηx​x​x+b​ηx​x​x​x​x=0,in​(0,L)×(0,T),η⁡(0,t)=η⁡(L,t)=ηx​(0,t)=ηx​(L,t)=0,in​(0,T),u⁡(0,t)=u⁡(L,t)=ux​(0,t)=ux​(L,t)=0,in​(0,T),ux​x​(0,t)+α1​ηx​x​(0,t)=0,in​(0,T),ux​x​(L,t)−α2​ηx​x​(L,t)=0,in​(0,T),η(x,0)=η0(x),u(x,0)=u0(x),in​(0,L).\begin{cases}\eta_{t}+u_{x}-au_{xxx}+bu_{xxxxx}=0,&\text{in}\,\,(0,L)\times(0,T),\\ u_{t}+\eta_{x}-a\eta_{xxx}+b\eta_{xxxxx}=0,&\text{in}\,\,(0,L)\times(0,T),\\ \eta(0,t)=\eta(L,t)=\eta_{x}(0,t)=\eta_{x}(L,t)=0,&\text{in}\,\,(0,T),\\ u(0,t)=u(L,t)=u_{x}(0,t)=u_{x}(L,t)=0,&\text{in}\,\,(0,T),\\ u_{xx}(0,t)+\alpha_{1}\eta_{xx}(0,t)=0,&\text{in}\,\,(0,T),\\ u_{xx}(L,t)-\alpha_{2}\eta_{xx}(L,t)=0,&\text{in}\,\,(0,T),\\ \eta(x,0)=\eta_{0}(x),\quad u(x,0)=u_{0}(x),&\text{in}\,\,(0,L).\end{cases}

We consider X0X_{0} with the usual inner product and the operator A:D⁡(A)⊂X0→X0A:D(A)\subset X_{0}\to X_{0} with domain

D(A)={(η,u)∈[H5(0,L)∩H02(0,L)]2:ux​x(0)+α1ηx​x(0)=0,ux​x(L)−α2ηx​x(L)=0},D(A)=\{(\eta,u)\in[H^{5}(0,L)\cap H^{2}_{0}(0,L)]^{2}:u_{xx}(0)+\alpha_{1}\eta_{xx}(0)=0,u_{xx}(L)-\alpha_{2}\eta_{xx}(L)=0\},

A⁡(η,u)=(−ux+a​ux​x​x−b​ux​x​x​x​x,−ηx+a​ηx​x​x−b​ηx​x​x​x​x).A(\eta,u)=(-u_{x}+au_{xxx}-bu_{xxxxx},-\eta_{x}+a\eta_{xxx}-b\eta_{xxxxx}).

Let us denote X5=D⁡(A)X_{5}=D(A). Moreover, we introduce the Hilbert space

X5​θ:=[X0,X5][θ],for 0<θ<5,X_{5\theta}:=[X_{0},X_{5}]_{[\theta]},\quad\text{for $0<\theta<5$},

where [X0,X5][θ][X_{0},X_{5}]_{[\theta]} denote the the Banach space obtained by the complex interpolation method (see, e.g., [3]).

Then, the following result holds:

Proposition 2.1.

If αi≥0\alpha_{i}\geq 0, i=1,2i=1,2, then AA generates a C0C_{0}-semigroup of contraction (S⁡(t))t≥0(S(t))_{t\geq 0} in X0X_{0}.

Proof.

Clearly, AA is densely defined and closed, so we are done if we prove that AA and its adjoint A∗A^{*} are both dissipative in X0X_{0}. It is easy to see that

The next result establishes the well-posedness of the non-homogeneous feedback linear system associated to (3.3).

Lemma 3.3.

Let T>0T>0. Then, for every (η0,u0)(\eta_{0},u_{0}) in X¯3\overline{X}_{3} and (h1,h2)(h_{1},h_{2}) in L2​(0,T,X−2)L^{2}(0,T;X_{-2}), there exists a unique solution (η,u)(\eta,u) of the system (3.3) such that

(η,u)∈C⁡([0,T],X¯3),(\eta,u)\in C([0,T];\overline{X}_{3}),

with f⁡(t):=−α1​ηx​x​(0,t)f(t):=-\alpha_{1}\eta_{xx}(0,t) and g⁡(t):=α2​ηx​x​(L,t)g(t):=\alpha_{2}\eta_{xx}(L,t), where α1\alpha_{1} and α2\alpha_{2} belong to ℝ\mathbb{R}. Moreover, for some positive constant C=C⁡(T)C=C(T), we have

‖(η⁡(t),u⁡(t))‖X¯3≤C⁡(‖(η0,u0)‖X¯3+‖(h1,h2)‖L2​(0,T,X−2)),∀t∈[0,T].\displaystyle\|(\eta(t),u(t))\|_{\overline{X}_{3}}\leq C\left(\|(\eta_{0},u_{0})\|_{\overline{X}_{3}}+\|(h_{1},h_{2})\|_{L^{2}(0,T;X_{-2})}\right),\quad\forall t\in[0,T].
Proof.

f⁡(t):=−α1​ηx​x​(0,t)​ and ​g​(t):=α2​ηx​x​(L,t)∈H−15​(0,T).f(t):=-\alpha_{1}\eta_{xx}(0,t)\text{ and }g(t):=\alpha_{2}\eta_{xx}(L,t)\in H^{-\frac{1}{5}}(0,T).

In fact, by using the continuous embedding L2​(0,T)⊂H−15​(0,T)L^{2}(0,T)\subset H^{-\frac{1}{5}}(0,T) and the trace theorem [1, Theorem 7.53], there exists a positive constant C:=C⁡(L,α1,α2)C:=C(L,\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}) such that

(3.21) ‖α1​ηx​x​(0,⋅)‖H−15​(0,T)2+‖α2​ηx​x​(L,⋅)‖H−15​(0,T)2≤C​∫0T(α12​ηx​x2​(0,t)+α22​ηx​x2​(L,t))​𝑑t≤C​∫0T‖η⁡(t)‖X¯32​𝑑t≤T​C​‖(η,u)‖C⁡([0,T],X¯3)2.\begin{split}\|\alpha_{1}\eta_{xx}(0,\cdot)\|_{{H^{-\frac{1}{5}}(0,T)}}^{2}+\|\alpha_{2}\eta_{xx}(L,\cdot)\|_{{H^{-\frac{1}{5}}(0,T)}}^{2}&\leq C\int_{0}^{T}\left(\alpha_{1}^{2}\eta_{xx}^{2}(0,t)+\alpha_{2}^{2}\eta_{xx}^{2}(L,t)\right)dt\\ &\leq C\int_{0}^{T}\|\eta(t)\|_{\overline{X}_{3}}^{2}dt\\ &\leq TC\|(\eta,u)\|_{C([0,T];\overline{X}_{3})}^{2}.\end{split}

Adapting the proof of Theorem 1.1, one can also prove, without any restriction over the initial data (η0,u0)(\eta_{0},u_{0}), that there exist T∗>0T^{*}>0 and a solution (η,u)(\eta,u) of (3.1)-(3.2), satisfying the initial condition η⁡(⋅,0)=η0​(⋅)\eta(\cdot,0)=\eta_{0}(\cdot) and u⁡(⋅,0)=u0​(⋅)u(\cdot,0)=u_{0}(\cdot). Let us now to prove Theorem 1.2 concerning of exponential stability for the linear system (2.1).

{λ​η0+u0′−a​u0′′′+b​u0′′′′′=0,in​(0,L),λ​u0+η0′−a​η0′′′+b​η0′′′′′=0,in​(0,L),η0​(0)=η0​(L)=η0′​(0)=η0′​(L)=η0′′​(0)=η0′′​(L)=0,u0​(0)=u0​(L)=u0′​(0)=u0′​(L)=u0′′​(0)=u0′′​(L)=0.\begin{split}\begin{cases}\lambda\eta_{0}+u^{\prime}_{0}-au^{\prime\prime\prime}_{0}+bu^{\prime\prime\prime\prime\prime}_{0}=0,&\text{in}\,\,(0,L),\\ \lambda u_{0}+\eta^{\prime}_{0}-a\eta^{\prime\prime\prime}_{0}+b\eta^{\prime\prime\prime\prime\prime}_{0}=0,&\text{in}\,\,(0,L),\\ \eta_{0}(0)=\eta_{0}(L)=\eta^{\prime}_{0}(0)=\eta^{\prime}_{0}(L)=\eta^{\prime\prime}_{0}(0)=\eta^{\prime\prime}_{0}(L)=0,\\ u_{0}(0)=u_{0}(L)=u^{\prime}_{0}(0)=u^{\prime}_{0}(L)=u^{\prime\prime}_{0}(0)=u^{\prime\prime}_{0}(L)=0.\end{cases}\end{split}

{λ​η+u′−a​u′′′+b​u′′′′′=0,in​(0,L),λ​u+η′−a​η′′′+b​η′′′′′=0,in​(0,L),η⁡(x)=η′​(x)=η′′​(x)=0,in​{0,L},u⁡(x)=u′​(x)=u′′​(x)=0,in​{0,L}.\begin{cases}\lambda\eta+u^{\prime}-au^{\prime\prime\prime}+bu^{\prime\prime\prime\prime\prime}=0,&\text{in}\,\,(0,L),\\ \lambda u+\eta^{\prime}-a\eta^{\prime\prime\prime}+b\eta^{\prime\prime\prime\prime\prime}=0,&\text{in}\,\,(0,L),\\ \eta(x)=\eta^{\prime}(x)=\eta^{\prime\prime}(x)=0,&\text{in}\,\,\{0,L\},\\ u(x)=u^{\prime}(x)=u^{\prime\prime}(x)=0,&\text{in}\,\,\{0,L\}.\end{cases}

Proof.

Firstly, let us consider the following change of variable φ⁡(x)=η⁡(x)±u⁡(x)\varphi(x)=\eta(x)\pm u(x), thus we have the problem in only one equation:

(4.10) {λ​φ+φ′−a​φ′′′+b​φ′′′′′=0,in​(0,L),φ⁡(x)=φ′​(x)=φ′′​(x)=0,in​{0,L}.\begin{cases}\lambda\varphi+\varphi^{\prime}-a\varphi^{\prime\prime\prime}+b\varphi^{\prime\prime\prime\prime\prime}=0,&\text{in}\,\,(0,L),\\ \varphi(x)=\varphi^{\prime}(x)=\varphi^{\prime\prime}(x)=0,&\text{in}\,\,\{0,L\}.\end{cases}

Note that, if we multiply the equation in (4.10) by φ¯\overline{\varphi} and integrate in [0,L][0,L], it is easy to see that λ\lambda is purely imaginary, i.e., λ=i​r\lambda=ir, for r∈ℝr\in\mathbb{R}. in 𝒮′​(ℝ){\mathcal{S}}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}), where δζ\delta_{\zeta} denotes the Dirac measure at x=ζx=\zeta and the derivatives φ′′′′​(0)\varphi^{\prime\prime\prime\prime}(0), φ′′′′​(L)\varphi^{\prime\prime\prime\prime}(L), φ′′′​(0)\varphi^{\prime\prime\prime}(0) and φ′′′​(L)\varphi^{\prime\prime\prime}(L) are those of the function φ\varphi when restricted to [0,L][0,L]. Taking the Fourier transform of each term in the above system and integrating by parts, we obtain

λ​φ^​(ξ)+i​ξ​φ^​(ξ)−a​(i​ξ)3​φ^​(ξ)+b​(i​ξ)5​φ^​(ξ)=b⁡(i​ξ)​φ′′′​(0)−b⁡(i​ξ)​φ′′′​(L)​e−i​L​ξ+b​φ′′′′​(0)−b​φ′′′′​(L)​e−i​L​ξ.\begin{split}\lambda\hat{\varphi}(\xi)+i\xi\hat{\varphi}(\xi)-a(i\xi)^{3}\hat{\varphi}(\xi)+b(i\xi)^{5}\hat{\varphi}(\xi)=&b(i\xi)\varphi^{\prime\prime\prime}(0)-b(i\xi)\varphi^{\prime\prime\prime}(L)e^{-iL\xi}\\ &+b\varphi^{\prime\prime\prime\prime}(0)-b\varphi^{\prime\prime\prime\prime}(L)e^{-iL\xi}.\end{split}

Setting λ=−i​r\lambda=-ir and fα​(ξ,L)=i​φ^​(ξ)f_{\alpha}(\xi,L)=i\hat{\varphi}(\xi), from the equation above it follows that

For each r∈ℝr\in\mathbb{R} and α∈ℂ4∖{0}\alpha\in\mathbb{C}^{4}\setminus\{0\} let ℱα​r\mathcal{F}_{\alpha r} be the set of L>0L>0 values, for which the function fα​(⋅,L)f_{\alpha}(\cdot,L) is entire. We introduce the following statements, which are equivalent:

The next claim analyzes the behavior of the roots of polynomial q⁡(⋅)q(\cdot):

Claim 1.

The polynomial q⁡(⋅)q(\cdot) has exactly one real root, with multiplicity 11 and two pairs of complex conjugate roots.

Proof of the Claim 1.

Initially, we suppose that r≠0r\neq 0. Note that the derivative of qq is given by

q′​(ξ)=5​b​ξ4+3​a​ξ2+1,q^{\prime}(\xi)=5b\xi^{4}+3a\xi^{2}+1,

and its zeros are ±z1\pm z_{1} and ±z2\pm z_{2}, where

z1=−3​a−9​a2−20​b10​bandz2=−3​a+9​a2−20​b10​b.z_{1}=\sqrt{\frac{-3a-\sqrt{9a^{2}-20b}}{10b}}\quad\text{and}\quad z_{2}=\sqrt{\frac{-3a+\sqrt{9a^{2}-20b}}{10b}}.

It is easy to see that z1z_{1} and z2z_{2} belong to ℂ∖ℝ\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{R}. Hence, the polynomial q⁡(⋅)q(\cdot) does not have critical points, which means that q⁡(⋅)q(\cdot) has exactly one real root. Suppose that ξ0∈ℝ\xi_{0}\in\mathbb{R} is the root of q⁡(⋅)q(\cdot) with multiplicity m≤5m\leq 5. Hence,

q⁡(ξ0)=q′​(ξ0)=…=q(m−1)​(ξ0)=0.q(\xi_{0})=q^{\prime}(\xi_{0})=...=q^{(m-1)}(\xi_{0})=0.

Consider the following cases:

  1. (i)

    If ξ0\xi_{0} has multiplicity 55, it follows that q⁡(ξ0)=0q(\xi_{0})=0 and q′′′′​(ξ0)=120​b​ξ0=0q^{\prime\prime\prime\prime}(\xi_{0})=120b\xi_{0}=0, implying that ξ0=0\xi_{0}=0 and r=0r=0.

  2. (ii)

    If ξ0\xi_{0} has multiplicity 44, it follows that q′′′​(ξ0)=60​b​ξ02+6​a=0q^{\prime\prime\prime}(\xi_{0})=60b\xi^{2}_{0}+6a=0, implying that ξ0∈i​ℝ\xi_{0}\in i\mathbb{R}.

  3. (iii)

    If ξ0\xi_{0} has multiplicity 33, it follows that q⁡(ξ0)=0q(\xi_{0})=0 and q′′​(ξ0)=20​b​ξ03+6​a​ξ0=0q^{\prime\prime}(\xi_{0})=20b\xi^{3}_{0}+6a\xi_{0}=0, implying that ξ0=0\xi_{0}=0 and r=0r=0 or ξ0∈i​ℝ\xi_{0}\in i\mathbb{R}.

  4. (iv)

    If ξ0\xi_{0} has multiplicity 44, it follows that q′​(ξ0)=5​b​ξ04+3​a​ξ2+1=0q^{\prime}(\xi_{0})=5b\xi^{4}_{0}+3a\xi_{2}+1=0, implying that ξ0∈ℂ∖ℝ.\xi_{0}\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{R}.

In any case, we have a contradiction, since r≠0r\neq 0 and ξ0∈ℝ\xi_{0}\in\mathbb{R}. Consequently, q⁡(⋅)q(\cdot) has exactly one real root, with multiplicity 11. This means that this polynomial has two pairs of complex conjugate roots.

 

Second, we suppose that r=0r=0. Initially, note that from the derivation of the model (see the Appendix) we have that 4​b>a24b>a^{2}. Then, we obtain that

q⁡(ξ)=ξ⁡(b​ξ4+a​ξ2+1),q(\xi)=\xi(b\xi^{4}+a\xi^{2}+1),

whose roots are 0,±ρ0,\pm\rho and ±k\pm k where

(4.14) ρ2=−a2​b+i​4​b−a22​bandk=−a2​b−i​4​b−a22​b=ρ2¯=ρ¯2.\rho^{2}=-\frac{a}{2b}+i\frac{\sqrt{4b-a^{2}}}{2b}\quad\text{and}\quad k=-\frac{a}{2b}-i\frac{\sqrt{4b-a^{2}}}{2b}=\overline{\rho^{2}}=\overline{\rho}^{2}.

Thus, q⁡(⋅)q(\cdot) has two pairs of complex conjugate roots and one real root, proving Claim 1. ∎

 

Besides of the Claim 1 the following two auxiliary lemmas are necessary to conclude the proof of the Lemma 4.2. Their proofs can be found in [20, Lemmas 2.1 and 2.2], thus we will omit them.

Lemma 4.3.

Let non null α∈ℂ4\alpha\in\mathbb{C}^{4} with d⁡(α)=0d(\alpha)=0 and L>0L>0 for d⁡(α)d(\alpha) defined in (4.12). Then, the set of the imaginary parts of the zeros of Nα​(⋅,L)N_{\alpha}(\cdot,L) in (4.11) has at most two elements.

Lemma 4.4.

For any L>0L>0, there is no Möbius transformation MM, such that

M⁡(ξ)=e−i​L​ξ,ξ∈{ξ1,ξ2,ξ¯1,ξ¯2},\displaystyle M(\xi)=e^{-iL\xi},\quad\xi\in\{\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\bar{\xi}_{1},\bar{\xi}_{2}\},

with ξ1,ξ2,ξ¯1,ξ¯2\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\bar{\xi}_{1},\bar{\xi}_{2} all distinct in ℂ\mathbb{C}.

Let us finish the proof of Lemma 4.2. To do this, we need to consider two cases:

  • i.

    d⁡(α)≠0d(\alpha)\neq 0;

  • ii.

    d⁡(α)=0d(\alpha)=0,

where d⁡(α)d(\alpha) was defined in (4.12).

In fact, if d⁡(α)≠0d(\alpha)\neq 0, we can defined the Möbius transformation. Let us assume, by contradiction, that there exists L>0L>0 such that the function fa​(⋅,L)f_{a}(\cdot,L) is entire. Then, all roots of the polynomial q⁡(⋅)q(\cdot) must satisfy (4.13), i.e., there exists a Möbius transformation that takes each root ξ0\xi_{0} of q⁡(⋅)q(\cdot) into e−i​L​ξ0e^{-iL\xi_{0}}. However, this contradicts Lemma 4.4 and proves that if (𝒩)(\mathcal{N}) holds then ℱα​r=∅\mathcal{F}_{\alpha r}=\emptyset for all r∈ℝr\in\mathbb{R}. On the other hand, suppose that d⁡(α)=0d(\alpha)=0 and note that by using the claim 1, we can conclude that the set of the imaginary parts of the polynomial q⁡(⋅)q(\cdot) has at least three elements, thus it follows from Lemma 4.3 that ℱα​r=∅\mathcal{F}_{\alpha r}=\emptyset for all r∈ℝr\in\mathbb{R}. Note that in both cases, we have that ℱα​r=∅\mathcal{F}_{\alpha r}=\emptyset, which implies that (𝒩)(\mathcal{N}) only has the trivial solution for any L>0L>0, and the proof of Lemma 4.2 is archived. ∎

5. Further comments and open problems

In this section considerations will be done regarding the fifth order Boussinesq system (1.2)-(1.3). It is important to note that the classical energy estimate does not provide any global (in time) a priori bounds for the solutions of the corresponding nonlinear model. Consequently, it does not lead to the existence of a global (in time) solution in the energy space. Due to the structure of the nonlinear terms, the same lack of a priori bounds also occurs when higher order Sobolev norms are considered (e. g. Hs−H^{s}-norm). Because to this strict requirement, we cannot proceed as in [10, 18] and have only succeeded in deriving uniform decay results for the linear system. However, for the full system, we can find solutions - in a certain sense - globally in time in X¯s\overline{X}_{s}.

∙\bullet Global well-posedness in time

Theorem 1.1 and Proposition 3.5 give us a positive answer to the well-posedness problem. However, the following questions are still open:

Question 𝒜\mathcal{A}.

Is the nonlinear system (1.2)-(1.3), global well-posedness in time? If yes, should we expect some restriction on the initial data?

∙\bullet One feedback on the boundary condition

If we consider in (1.2)-(1.3) with only one damping mechanism, that is, with α1\alpha_{1} or α2\alpha_{2} vanishing, we still have E⁡(t)E(t), defined by (1.4), decreasing along the trajectories of the linearized system associated to the model. Thus, the following question can be formulated:

Question 𝒞\mathcal{C}.

Is still valid, with only one damping mechanism, the exponential stability for the linearized system associated to (1.2)-(1.3)?

∙\bullet Exponential stability for the full system

Due the lack of the classical energy estimate for the nonlinear model we are not able to prove, by using, e.g., [10, 18], the exponential stability for the full model (1.2)-(1.3). Then, one natural question remains open:

Question ℰ\mathcal{E}.

Does the energy associated to the nonlinear system (1.2)-(1.3), with one or two damping mechanism, converges to zero, as t→∞t\rightarrow\infty, for initial data on the energy space X0X_{0}?
